title: PromQL in depth: rates, aggregation and recording rules
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A counter only goes up, so its raw value is rarely useful.
`sum by (service)(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))` keeps only the service label.
Histogram buckets are counters, so use `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, service)(rate(latency_bucket[5m])))`.
A series that stops appearing is marked stale after five minutes, and a missing scrape leaves a gap.
Expensive expressions evaluated by every dashboard refresh waste CPU.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A dashboard that averaged quantiles
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
The p99 latency graph looked fine while customers complained about slow requests.
An operator runs a command such as: curl -s localhost:9090/api/v1/query --data-urlencode 'query=avg(service_latency_p99_seconds)'
The first query averaged the p99 of each instance, which is not the p99 of all requests.
The second merges the buckets and shows a real p99 of 1.84 seconds.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Using rate on a gauge or summing before rate.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Scaling Prometheus: HA, federation and long-term storage
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Memory use is driven mostly by active series, and each series costs a few kilobytes.
Run two identical replicas that scrape the same targets.
When one server cannot hold all series, shard targets across servers by a hash or by team.
Thanos sidecars upload blocks to object storage and a store gateway serves them back for queries.
Alert on head series growth, WAL replay time, rejected samples and slow rule evaluations.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: The label that added ten million series
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A deployment added a per-request id as a label and Prometheus ran out of memory in an hour.
An operator runs a command such as: curl -s localhost:9090/api/v1/status/tsdb | head -c 220
The request id label created a new series for every request.
The label was dropped with a relabel rule, the server was restarted from its last good state and a limit on samples per scrape was added so one target cannot do this again.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Running one server with no replica for critical alerts.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: SLO alerting: burn rates and Alertmanager design
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A 99.9 percent monthly SLO leaves 0.1 percent of requests as budget.
A fast alert uses a short window and a high burn rate, such as 14.4 over one hour and five minutes, and pages someone.
Alertmanager routes by labels to receivers.
Group alerts by service so one outage creates one notification.
Review each page: was it actionable, urgent and real?
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: Two hundred pages from one outage
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A database failure triggered a separate page for every dependent service.
An operator runs a command such as: amtool alert query --active | wc -l
Grouping by instance meant every pod produced its own notification.
Grouping by service, adding an inhibition rule from the database alert to dependent alerts and moving most conditions to ticket routes reduced the next incident to three pages.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Paging on causes such as CPU instead of user impact.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Logs at scale: Loki, labels and retention
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Loki indexes only labels such as namespace, app and level, and stores the log text compressed in chunks.
Do not use user ids, request ids or pod names with churn as labels.
A query starts with a stream selector such as `{app="api", env="prod"}`, then filters with `|= "error"` or parses with `| json`.
Keep recent logs on fast storage and older logs in cheap object storage with a retention period per tenant or stream.
Add a trace id to each log line and configure the data source to link it to the trace view.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: Logs rejected for too many streams
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A new label caused Loki to reject writes and logs went missing during an outage.
An operator runs a command such as: logcli series '{app="api"}' --analyze-labels | head -4
The agent added the pod uid as a label, so every restart created a new stream and the limit on active streams was hit.
Removing that label and keeping app, env and namespace restored ingestion.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Using request or user ids as labels.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Distributed tracing: sampling and correlation
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Each unit of work is a span with a start, a duration and attributes.
The decision is made at the start of the request, for example keep one percent.
A collector holds the whole trace for a short period and then decides: keep all errors, keep traces slower than a threshold and keep a small share of the rest.
Look for the longest span on the critical path, repeated spans such as the same query run many times and gaps where no span exists.
Exemplars attach a trace id to a metric sample so a latency histogram can link to a real slow trace.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: Traces that ended at the queue
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
Slow checkouts could not be traced past the message queue.
An operator runs a command such as: kubectl logs deploy/otel-collector | grep -c "orphan span"
The producer did not copy the trace context into the message headers, so the consumer started a new trace.
Adding context injection and extraction around the queue joined the traces and revealed the real delay in the payment service.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Sampling one percent at random and missing the slow requests.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Observability as code and cost control
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Store Grafana dashboards as JSON or generated from a library, and alert rules as files, in version control.
An OpenTelemetry Collector configuration lists receivers, processors and exporters.
Every metric, log stream and dashboard should have an owner label or folder.
Cost comes from active series for metrics, ingested gigabytes for logs and sampled spans for traces.
Each quarter, list dashboards with no views and alerts that never fired or always fire, and decide to delete or fix them.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A dashboard edit that disappeared
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A team fixed a panel in the UI and the fix vanished the next day.
An operator runs a command such as: git log --oneline -3 -- dashboards/payments.json
The dashboard is provisioned from the repository, so the UI edit was overwritten by the next deploy.
The fix was committed as a pull request, and the provisioning settings now mark UI editing as disabled with a note linking to the repository.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Editing provisioned dashboards by hand.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
